title: How sea turtles find their way home
text:
Every year, on beaches from Sumatra to Papua, female sea turtles drag themselves out of the surf under cover of darkness. Each one digs a deep hole in the sand with her back flippers, lays around a hundred soft, round eggs, covers them carefully and returns to the sea. She will never see her babies. Yet, remarkably, many females come back to nest on or near the same stretch of coast where they hatched, even after swimming thousands of kilometres across the ocean.

Scientists are still learning how turtles manage this. One idea is that they sense the Earth's magnetic field, which varies slightly from place to place along a coastline. The turtle may remember the magnetic "signature" of her birthplace, rather like an invisible address. Researchers have tested this by placing young turtles in tanks with changed magnetic fields. The turtles swam in different directions, which suggests that they do use magnetism to steer.

The eggs stay buried for about two months. The temperature of the sand matters a great deal during this time. Warmer sand tends to produce more female hatchlings, while cooler sand produces more males. Because the climate is warming, some nesting beaches now produce far more females than males, and conservationists are watching this carefully.

When the hatchlings finally break out, they usually emerge at night, when the sand is cooler and fewer birds are hunting. They scramble towards the sea by heading for the brightest horizon, which, on a natural beach, is the open water reflecting the sky. Bright streetlamps and hotel lights can fool them. Instead of reaching the waves, some hatchlings crawl towards the road and are lost.

Because of this, many beach communities now switch off or shield their lights during nesting season. Volunteers walk the sand at dawn to find nests, and some move eggs to protected hatcheries where they can be guarded from predators and people. In many places, rangers also let local children release the hatchlings, so that the next generation of villagers grows up caring for the turtles.

Only a few hatchlings survive to become adults. The ones that do can live for decades and, one day, they follow the same mysterious map back to the beach where their own lives began.
